title: About
text:
Jason Smith is a Professor of Public Health at California State University, Fullerton. He has served in senior academic leadership roles at CSUF and CSU East Bay, including Dean of the College of Health and Human Development at CSUF and Chair of the Department of Public Health at CSU East Bay, and completed an American Council on Education Fellowship in the Office of Chancellor Cindy Larive at UC Santa Cruz. He has held teaching appointments at the University of Connecticut Health Center and Northeastern University School of Law. Professor Smith’s current scholarship examines public health law and climate governance, with a focus on constitutional frameworks for intergenerational justice and the legal status of population health as a norm. His work has appeared in leading law and public health journals, and he serves on the Board of Directors of the American Society of Law, Medicine, and Ethics. He is a licensed attorney in California and Massachusetts. He holds a JD from Northeastern University School of Law and an MTS from Harvard University.

title: Research
text: My research stands at the intersection of public health, law, and climate governance, and asks the question: How can governance systems adapt to the public health implications of climate change while reducing inequities? I argue constitutional law as a field and as a practice can and should be the site of the practice of public health. Work in public health and in law has largely treated these two fields as related but separate domains and has treated the issues of climate change as technical adaptation issues. The public health challenges of the Anthropocene are fundamentally governance challenges that require not only technical adaptation and mitigation measures but also fundamental shifts in jurisprudence and a recognition of the significant overlap of public health and law as fields. This area of focus is an extension of my use of population-based legal analysis in US public health law into comparative constitutional law and jurisprudence. I draw on the German Schutzpflichten tradition and the Neubauer decision and its development of the doctrine of intertemporal freedom guarantee as doctrinal resources that public health law has lacked. I consider the possibilities of population-based legal analysis and populations as more than interpretive frameworks by reconceiving the carbon budget as population health and population health as constitutional and intertemporal.

title: Jason Smith
text:
Biography
I am a professor in the Department of Public Health at California State University, Fullerton. My work and interests are on the legal and ethical aspects of public health and climate change. I have written on heat action plans in California, emphasizing the need for effective governance to address the health impacts of extreme heat, public health surveillance, and public health law generally. I am licensed to practice law in Massachusetts (2003) and in California (2025).
